content: The study involved 266,939 participants, with a median proportion of 47% males across the studies. These individuals were followed for a total of 1,837,794 person-years. The results demonstrated consistency between unadjusted odds ratios and both adjusted and unadjusted relative risks or hazard ratios. No significant moderators were identified. Although publication bias was detected, adjusting for this did not alter the strength of the associations observed. The findings support the conclusion that physical activity provides protective benefits against the onset of depression, regardless of age or geographical location. Physical activity was defined as any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure. Depression outcomes were assessed using standardized instruments, diagnostic interviews, or physician diagnoses. The population analyzed included adults of any age who were free of depression or depressive symptoms at baseline. No funding sources were reported by the authors. A meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies also examined the relationship between physical activity and the risk of developing anxiety. The analysis found that higher levels of physical activity were associated with a reduced risk of anxiety, including specific conditions such as agoraphobia and post-traumatic stress disorder. The protective effects of physical activity were consistent across demographic factors. Another study investigated the association between meeting U.S. federal physical activity guidelines and mortality risk among smokers. The analysis, which included data from the 1998–2009 National Health Interview Surveys linked to the National Death Index, found that meeting both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activity recommendations was associated with reduced all-cause, cardiovascular, cancer, and respiratory disease mortality risks. These findings highlight the importance of promoting adherence to physical activity guidelines, particularly among smokers. A separate pooled analysis examined the unique health benefits of strength-promoting exercises (SPE) compared to aerobic activity. Using data from the Health Survey for England and the Scottish Health Survey, the study found that adherence to SPE guidelines (≥2 sessions per week) was associated with reduced all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality. The results emphasize the value of incorporating strength exercises into public health recommendations. A systematic review and meta-analysis explored the effects of physically active video games (exergames) on cognitive functioning in clinical and non-clinical populations. The analysis included 17 randomized controlled trials with 926 participants and found that exergames improved overall cognition, executive functions, attentional processing, and visuospatial skills. These findings suggest that exergames may serve as a novel strategy to enhance cognitive functioning, though further research is needed to identify factors influencing their efficacy and underlying neurobiological mechanisms. Another systematic review investigated the impact of evening exercise on sleep quality. Contrary to common recommendations against evening exercise, the analysis found no evidence that evening physical activity negatively affects sleep. In fact, moderate evening exercise may improve sleep quality, although vigorous exercise ending within one hour of bedtime could impair sleep onset latency, total sleep time, and sleep efficiency. A meta-analysis evaluated the effects of low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on body composition and cardiorespiratory fitness. The findings indicated that while low-volume HIIT is not effective for reducing total body fat mass or percentage compared to non-exercise controls or moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT), it significantly improves cardiorespiratory fitness. This suggests that low-volume HIIT is a time-efficient method for enhancing fitness but not for altering body composition. Finally, a systematic review assessed the effectiveness of Tai Chi in improving quality of life among perimenopausal women. The analysis found that Tai Chi significantly improved dimensions such as bodily pain, general health, vitality, and mental health, as well as bone mineral density in the spine. These results suggest that Tai Chi may be a safe and effective adjunctive treatment for perimenopausal syndrome, though more high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings.
